nameStory: Prairie moonwort gets its name from its natural habitat in prairie grasslands and its distinctive crescent-shaped leaflets that reminded early botanists of phases of the moon. The 'wort' part is an old English word meaning 'plant' or 'herb,' commonly used in traditional plant names.
description: Prairie moonwort is a tiny, unusual fern that looks more like a small wildflower than what most people think of as a fern. This diminutive plant typically stands just a few inches tall and has a single, delicate frond divided into small, rounded segments. Instead of the typical fern look, it produces a separate stalk topped with tiny spore-bearing structures that give it an almost alien appearance. It's one of the rarest ferns you might encounter in New England.

idTips.label: Fronds
idTips.description: Single triangular frond divided into small, rounded to oval segments that feel delicate and thin to the touch, often with a slightly waxy surface

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Extremely small stature, usually under 4 inches tall, emerging as a solitary plant rather than in clusters

idTips.label: Sori
idTips.description: Spores produced on a separate, upright stalk that branches into tiny grape-like clusters, completely different from typical fern sori

idTips.label: Stipe
idTips.description: Short, smooth stem that's often pale green to yellowish and feels firm but fragile when gently touched

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in dry, sandy or gravelly soils in prairie-like openings, often among grasses in areas with poor, well-drained soil

habitat: Prairie moonwort prefers dry, sandy or gravelly soils in open areas that mimic prairie conditions, such as old fields, sandy barrens, or disturbed sites with sparse vegetation. In New England, it's most likely to be found in areas with well-drained, nutrient-poor soils where grasses and low-growing plants dominate. It seems to favor slightly alkaline conditions and areas that experience periodic disturbance.

seasonality.spring: Fronds begin emerging in late spring, appearing as small, distinctive shoots that don't look like typical fern fiddleheads.
seasonality.summer: Peak visibility occurs in early to mid-summer when both the leaf and spore-bearing stalk are fully developed and easiest to spot.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to yellow and die back, becoming increasingly difficult to locate as surrounding vegetation changes color.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant and invisible above ground, leaving no trace until the following spring's emergence.

funFact: Prairie moonwort was only discovered and described by science in the 1980s, making it one of the most recently discovered fern species in North America, and it's so rare that some botanists go their entire careers without seeing one in the wild.
confusionNotes: Its tiny size and unusual appearance mean it's more likely to be overlooked entirely than confused with other ferns. When noticed, beginners might mistake it for a small wildflower seedling rather than a fern, since it lacks the typical feathery fern appearance.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting prairie habitat, prairie moonwort represents a fascinating example of how some 'prairie' plants have found refuge in New England's scattered dry, open habitats that ecologically resemble prairie conditions, even though true prairies don't naturally occur in this region.
compareHints: Prairie moonwort is distinguished from other moonworts by its preference for dry, prairie-like conditions rather than the moist, shaded habitats preferred by most of its relatives. Its frond segments are more rounded and less divided than those of matricary grapefern, and it's typically found in much drier sites than swamp moonwort. The tiny little grapefern is similar in size but has more deeply cut, narrow segments rather than the rounded leaflets of prairie moonwort.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Matricary grapefern is distinguished from other moonworts by its chamomile-like leaf segments that are more finely divided than most of its relatives.
Narrow triangle moonwort differs from matricary grapefern by having much narrower, more pointed segments rather than finely dissected, lacy ones.
**[Uncertain claim flagged: specific comparison details]** Swamp moonwort is distinguished from other moonworts by its preference for wet habitats and its small, fan-shaped sterile frond segments.
Little grapefern is distinguished from other moonworts by its simple, often undivided leaf blade, whereas matricary grapefern and others have multiple leaflets or more complex divisions.

Upswept moonwort differs from other moonworts by its fan or wedge-shaped leaflet segments that angle upward, rather than the more rounded or deeply divided segments of relatives like matricary grapefern.
Unlike its moonwort relatives with their more typical triangular or oval leaflet shapes, spathulate moonwort's spatula-shaped segments are unmistakable.
